lesson.title: Research symposium: build a conference-style research story
lesson.short: Claim · mechanism · evidence · limitations · group handoffs
lesson.timeMeaning: Suggested independent study minutes; not scheduled contact time
lesson.lead: Your audience should leave knowing the problem, the idea, the evidence and the condition under which the idea stops helping.
goals: Organize a talk around one supported claim.
Explain a mechanism with a small worked example before benchmarks.
Design readable evidence slides and coordinated group handoffs.

sections.title: Start here: prerequisites and course status
sections.html:
“Our system is twice as fast” is memorable, but an audience cannot tell whether it helps a user. We will build a short argument from two arriving queries, then connect it to a clearly labeled hypothetical benchmark claim.

Bring one supported claim, its evidence and a failure case. This supplemental symposium practice is not an Edinburgh lecture or verified Canvas assignment. Presentation length, question period, contribution reporting, assessment and submission instructions remain unverified; use actual instructor instructions when supplied.

sections.title: The research story in four questions
sections.html:
An audience first needs the problem: what do users wait for? Then the bottleneck: why does the current path struggle? Then the mechanism: what changes operationally? Finally the evidence: what was measured under which conditions? These four questions form an argument the listener can reconstruct.

For our ANN example, name the workload, resource boundary and recall requirement at the start. Reuse a few queries to show immediate dispatch and batching. Explain the added waiting cost along with reduced device work. If a listener can predict when batching loses, they understand more than a headline.

Choose one central claim and supporting observations. Implementation history belongs only when it explains a decision or failure. A chronological diary of debugging makes listeners assemble the argument themselves; show them the causal path directly.

Key takeaway

A clear talk lets the audience reconstruct the argument, not just remember the headline.

sections.title: An adaptable presentation outline
sections.html:
Start the talk with the question and scope. Show a baseline trace so the bottleneck is visible. Introduce one operational change, then state the methodology needed to test it: dataset, baseline, resources, quality target and timing boundary.

Only then show the main comparison, with units and uncertainty large enough to read. Follow it with an ablation or counterexample explaining why the change helps and where it does not. End with the supported answer, a specific limitation and an artifact path.

This is an adaptable sequence, not mandatory slide headings. Fit it to the actual allotted time rather than inventing course timing. Rehearse by asking whether each transition resolves a question raised on the preceding slide. If a chart needs many unexplained definitions, introduce a small worked example before it.

sections.title: Worked example: replace a headline with an argument
sections.html:
Original mechanism trace: Q1 arrives at 0 ms and Q2 at 1 ms. Immediate serial execution takes 2 ms each. Q1 runs 0–2, Q2 runs 2–4; response times are 2−0=2 and 4−1=3 ms.

Batching waits until 1 ms, then processes both in an assumed 2 ms. Both finish at 3 ms. Response times are 3−0=3 and 3−1=2 ms. The pair finishes earlier, but the first query waits longer. If only Q1 arrives, the same 1 ms wait plus 2 ms execution gives 3 ms instead of 2 ms with no batching benefit. These supplied costs illustrate a mechanism; they do not derive the benchmark numbers below.

A stronger hypothetical claim than “2× faster” is: on a fixed public million-vector workload, batching raises throughput from 8,000 to 16,000 queries/s at recall@10=0.95, while p95 response latency rises from 4 to 7 ms. It doubles throughput at that quality but increases latency. Name arrival pattern, hardware, timing boundary, failures and uncertainty before presenting such numbers as your own measurements.

Why is this stronger even though it admits a cost?

The audience can decide whether throughput matters enough and whether 7 ms meets their latency budget. A throughput-only headline cannot answer that user question.

sections.title: Group presentation as one coherent explanation
sections.html:
Divide speaking roles by the argument rather than by source files. One person can introduce the question and baseline, another the mechanism, another methodology/results. Each still needs to know the central claim and limitation so transitions preserve meaning.

Agree on terms, units, colors and notation. A useful transition carries a question: “The trace predicts fewer transfers; now we test whether transfers dominate real latency.” Practice it with the next speaker, not as an isolated sentence.

Record actual contributions accurately instead of inventing equal participation or saying someone ran an experiment they did not. Keep a coordination list for order and backups. A failed live demo can be replaced by an explicitly recorded trace or screenshot; do not label a recording live. Follow confirmed course contribution requirements separately.

sections.title: Citations, backup evidence and rehearsal
sections.html:
A reused algorithm, figure or reported external result needs a visible short source and full citation/link. Label author-reported numbers separately from your experiments. Check figure/data licenses or make an original explanation of the underlying idea.

Prepare backup evidence for data splits, baseline tuning, hardware, quality, failures, ablations and raw traces. Rehearse once for logic, once for actual timing and once with skeptical questions. Ask an unfamiliar listener to restate both claim and limitation; inability to do so shows where the explanation needs repair.

You need a paper's chart but did not reproduce it. What can you say?

Attribute it as the authors' reported result with its conditions. Do not merge it into your measured series. Follow reuse permission or draw an original summary.

A demo fails in rehearsal. What is the useful next step?

Diagnose and record the failure, narrow unsupported claims and prepare a clearly labeled saved trace. Hiding failure removes evidence about reliability and leaves no plan when it happens again.

Key takeaway

A polished presentation makes assumptions and limits easier to see.

quiz.question: Which main-result slide is most defensible?
options: A comparison stating workload, baseline, units, quality target and uncertainty.
A speedup with no baseline name.
An unlabeled best-case screenshot.
A paper’s plot labeled as the group’s own result.
quiz.explanation: A scientific comparison needs enough context to interpret what improved and what was held fixed.

questions.question: Why show a small worked example before a benchmark chart?
options: It replaces all need for evaluation.
It helps the audience understand the mechanism and predict its limits.
It proves the method is novel.
It guarantees the demo will run.
questions.explanation: An operational example explains what changes and why the result might hold, while the benchmark provides separate evidence.
questions.origin: Original supplemental exercise; not a verified assessed question

questions.question: Which use of another paper’s plot is acceptable scientific communication?
options: Crop away the axes and citation.
Use its best number without mentioning conditions.
Attribute the original source, distinguish it from group measurements and respect reuse rights.
Label it as the group’s new result.
questions.explanation: Attribution and scope distinguish contextual prior evidence from the group’s own experiment; reuse rights still apply.
questions.origin: Original supplemental exercise; not a verified assessed question

questions.question: How should hypothetical numerical examples appear?
options: Hidden in a chart to improve appearance.
As measured results if they seem plausible.
Mixed with actual data without distinction.
Clearly labeled as illustrative invented numbers.
questions.explanation: Illustrative arithmetic is useful, but it must never be represented as experimental evidence.
questions.origin: Original supplemental exercise; not a verified assessed question

questions.question: What is a sensible group handoff?
options: A sudden switch to unrelated implementation history.
A transition connecting the current mechanism to the next evidence question.
A repeated introduction with no link to the argument.
An assertion that only one member knows the results.
questions.explanation: A coordinated handoff preserves the logical thread of the presentation.
